# slopball — next version

DERIVED by `make next-version` from .wire-changes/ and the last tag. Nothing
here ran: this tool never tags and never pushes, the same way
`make deploy-checklist` never runs wrangler. Cutting the release is yours.

  last tag       v0.1.0
  pending        3 entries — 1 breaking, 1 additive, 1 patch
  next version   v1.0.0
  why            a `breaking` entry is pending — an already-installed client
                 stops working, so the major moves.

## The changelog

The entries' own sentences, verbatim. `make next-version-consume` appends
exactly these bytes to CHANGELOG.md and deletes the entries — there is no
second write-up, so there is nothing to drift.

```markdown
## v1.0.0

### Breaking — an already-installed client stops working

- floor v1.4.0 — An old client is refused: the control plane no longer reads overlayAddr from a claim.

### Additive — an already-installed client is unaffected

- An old client keeps working: the control plane accepts a member row that carries no memberRole.

### Patch — nothing an already-installed client can observe changed

- An old client sees no difference: the field it never decoded was renamed.
```

## The sequence

Consume, then commit, then tag — in that order, so the tag points at a tree
whose CHANGELOG.md already says what shipped and whose ledger is empty.

```sh
make next-version-consume
git add -A && git commit -m "release v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```

The number is derived, not decided: it is max(class) over the pending entries,
and an empty ledger is a patch because a release changes more than the wire. It
is still a suggestion — tag something else if a release needs a number for a
reason the wire cannot see, and the next derivation reads whatever tag it finds.
